opinions.rationale: The narrow identification concern is correct: performance on selected trial-database pairs does not nonparametrically identify performance for a new question or database without a defined target distribution, a sampling or selection model, conditional exchangeability of benchmark performance, and positivity over the relevant design and setting modifiers. The assertion that there is "no theory" or "no design" is too absolute. Transport and hierarchical prediction are possible under explicit assumptions, although a hierarchical model cannot identify extrapolation outside observed support merely by conditioning on study features. Correlation is also not an agreement measure: it can be high despite systematic bias and low because of restricted effect variation or sampling error. Freezing the protocol prospectively blocks outcome-informed design adaptation only if all analytic choices are locked; it does not by itself prevent selective reporting after unblinding. The problem remains open in its narrower form because the supplied agenda does not provide an identified and validated transfer procedure. Its very-high severity is warranted only when benchmarking is used to certify decisions beyond the benchmarked design class.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: A successful replication identifies calibration only for the evaluated trial, protocol, and database. Quantitative transfer to another question or database requires a prespecified target performance estimand, an explicit selection or transport model, conditional exchangeability, and overlap in relevant modifiers; outside that support, transfer is model-dependent rather than identified.

opinions.rationale: The criticism of confidence-interval overlap and sign agreement is technically sound, but the problem is framed too broadly. The agenda's own descriptions say that the cited benchmarks already report several graded metrics, including effect correlation and standardized differences, so benchmarking is not uniformly binary. Continuous effect differences, ratios, and standardized contrasts still cannot separate estimand mismatch from random error. That separation first requires commensurate estimands and then a joint sampling model incorporating uncertainty from both estimates, their covariance when applicable, and between-pair heterogeneity. Prediction-interval coverage does not require a trial to publish a full error distribution when an estimate and standard error or confidence interval are available, and coverage is itself calibrated across a suite rather than diagnosed from one pair. Ratios are additionally unstable when the reference effect is near zero. This is therefore partly an implementation and reporting problem with existing tools, not wholly an unresolved statistical-method problem; high severity is disproportionate unless the binary label is the sole basis for a decision.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Binary replication labels based on interval overlap or effect direction discard magnitude and uncertainty and cannot diagnose why estimates differ. Decision-grade benchmarking should first align estimands, then report paired contrasts with joint uncertainty, heterogeneity, and prespecified tolerances whenever a categorical judgment is required.

resolving_work.title: Emulation of Randomized Clinical Trials With Nonrandomized Database Analyses: Results of 32 Clinical Trials
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: As characterized in the batch, this program reports several agreement metrics rather than only a binary replication label, partially resolving the reporting problem while not separating all sources of discrepancy.
